 Along with state and national elections, voters in parts of St. Croix County will decide four local referendums Nov. 3.
 The city and town of Hudson each have a referendum tied to Hudson Fire Department staffing, and the Somerset and Glenwood City school districts are seeking to exceed state revenue limits to cover operational costs.
 Voters will also help decide on three statewide constitutional amendments. Read our guide for those questions here.
 City of Hudson: fire department personnel referendum
 Verbatim:  “Under state law, the increase in the levy of the City of Hudson for the tax to be imposed for the next fiscal year, 2027, is limited to 0.872%, which results in a levy of $13,335,657. Shall the City of Hudson be allowed to exceed this limit and increase the levy for the next fiscal year, 2027, for the purpose of improving emergency services with 9 additional full-time fire staff and ongoing Hudson Fire Department expenses, by a total of 9.698%, which results in a levy of $14,628,943 and on an ongoing basis, include the increase of $1,293,285.68 for each fiscal year going forward?”
 Plain English: Do you support a permanent property tax increase to fund nine additional firefighters and ongoing department costs? 
 Background:  The Hudson City Council voted to place a referendum on the ballot to exceed its levy. The city is asking for a $1.29 million increase in the property tax levy — a permanent increase with an estimated impact of $37.34 per $100,000 of assessed value.
 The fire department has struggled to maintain adequate response times amid a recent uptick in the population of the city and the overall service area. Mueller Communications, a firm hired by the city, stated in its needs assessment that Hudson had an average response time of a little under 17 minutes for its first fire truck, compared to the industry standard of four minutes.
 Town of Hudson: town’s portion of fire department costs
 Verbatim:  “Under state law, the increase in the levy of the Town of Hudson for the tax to be imposed for the next fiscal year, 2027, is limited to 1.079%, which results in a levy of $1,314,542. Shall the Town of Hudson be allowed to exceed this limit and increase the levy for the next fiscal year, 2027, for the purpose of paying the increased costs of emergency services imposed by our contract with the City of Hudson, which has decided to add 9 full time firefighters and other associated expenses to reduce response times and provide improved emergency services, by a total of 37.474%, which results in a levy of $1,807,154, and on an ongoing basis, include the increase of $492,612 for each fiscal year going forward?”
 Plain English:  Do you support a permanent property tax increase to pay the town’s share of additional full-time firefighters?
 Background:  The Hudson Fire Department serves the city, the town of Hudson, the village of North Hudson and part of the town of Troy under contracts that run through 2040. If city voters approve their referendum, each partner must pay its share of the new positions.
 Each municipality’s share is based half on its property value and half on its call volume over the past five years. The city, with the largest tax base and the most calls, pays about 54% of operating costs, according to the fire department. The town of Hudson pays just under 24% , according to the town.
 North Hudson and Troy cover the rest. Neither placed a referendum on the ballot in November. North Hudson charges its share as a user fee. Troy plans to absorb about $120,000 from reserves in 2027 if the city’s referendum passes, according to staff.
 The town of Hudson estimates the increase at $23.43 per $100,000 of equalized value, or about $94 a year on a $400,000 home. If the city’s referendum passes and the town’s does not, the town would still owe its share under the contract and would “be forced to use borrowing and make significant cuts to other local services (such as parks and road maintenance) to fulfill this legal obligation,” according to its website.
 However, if the inverse happens — the city’s doesn’t pass and the town’s does — the town stated it will not raise the levy.
 Somerset School District: funding staff, maintenance
 Verbatim:  “Shall the School District of Somerset, located in St. Croix County, Wisconsin, be authorized to exceed the revenue limit specified in Section 121.91, Wisconsin Statutes, by $1,400,000 per year for five years, beginning with the 2027-2028 school year and ending with the 2031-2032 school year, for non-recurring purposes consisting of operational expenses, including but not limited to staffing, facility maintenance, and maintaining programs and services?”
 Plain English:  Do you support a temporary property tax increase to fund school operating costs such as staffing and building maintenance?
 Background:   The Somerset School Board approved a ballot question asking residents to let the district exceed its revenue limit by $1.4 million a year for five years, which expires after the 2031-32 school year unless voters approve another.
 The district projects a deficit of more than $1.4 million over five years, citing state aid not keeping pace with inflation and declining enrollment, according to its website. If passed, funding would maintain current programs and staffing and pay for maintenance.
 If it fails, the district says it would need to raise class sizes, cut programs and staff, freeze wages and defer maintenance.
 Glenwood City School District: avoiding future cuts
 Verbatim:  “Shall the School District of Glenwood City, St. Croix and Dunn Counties, Wisconsin be authorized to exceed the revenue limit specified in Section 121.91, Wisconsin Statutes, by $750,000 per year for four years, beginning with the 2026-2027 school year and ending with the 2029-2030 school year, for non-recurring purposes consisting of operational and maintenance expenses?”
 Plain English:  Do you support a property tax increase to cover operating and maintenance costs?
 Background:  The Glenwood City School Board voted to place a referendum on the ballot that would let the district exceed its revenue limit by $750,000 a year for four years. The district projects minimal to no increase in its overall tax rate, which it aims to keep near $7 per $1,000 of equalized value, though it says the final rate depends on state aid, property values and other factors.
 Glenwood City Schools has cut nearly $1 million in spending since 2023, according to the referendum flyer. However, it still projects a gap of around $2.5 million over four years, which the district has attributed to rising health insurance costs, an aging bus fleet, facility needs and declining enrollment.
 The referendum failing would likely lead to more program cuts and possibly staff cuts, a greater reliance on the fund balance and class size increases, the flyer stated. The district might also have to defer more maintenance, leading to higher costs. Without the funding from the referendum, “deeper cuts may be required in the future.”
